## sparsify_select - Sparsify Select {#sparsify_select}


The SparsifySelectPass is a type of range analysis-informed dead code
elimination that removes cases from selects when range analysis proves that
they can never occur. It does this by splitting a select into many selects,
each of which covers a single interval from the selector interval set.

!!! NOTE
    What follows was generated by the Gemini LLM. Not human verified.

The `SparsifySelectPass` uses range analysis to eliminate unreachable cases
from `select` operations. When the set of possible values that a `select`'s
selector can take covers fewer points than the number of cases in the
`select`, this pass replaces the original `select` with a smaller `select`
(or a chain of `select`s, one per reachable interval) that only indexes into
the reachable cases.

Here is a detailed breakdown of its operation:

1.  **Range Analysis**: The pass populates a `PartialInfoQueryEngine` and
    queries `GetIntervals(select->selector()).Get({})` to obtain the
    `IntervalSet` of possible values for the selector of each `Select` node.

2.  **Sparsity Check**: If the total number of values in the `IntervalSet`
    (`selector_intervals.Size()`) is strictly less than
    `select->cases().size()`, then at least one case in the `select` is
    provably unreachable.

3.  **Splitting into Per-Interval Selects (`SparsifySelect`)**:
    *   `IntervalsSortedBySize` sorts the convex intervals in
        `selector_intervals` from smallest to largest (breaking ties by
        interval order).
    *   For each reachable `Interval` `[lower, upper]`, the pass collects the
        corresponding slice of cases from the original `select` (using
        `select->default_value()` for indices `>= select->cases().size()`, or
        skipping the interval if it lies entirely past the end of `cases()`
        and no `default_value` is present).
    *   It constructs an inner `select` for the interval:
        `if_in_range = sel(sub(selector, lower), cases=cases_in_range,
        default=0)`.
    *   For the first interval processed (`is_leaf == true`), `if_in_range`
        is used directly without a range-check comparator (if the selector
        falls in no other interval, it must fall in this leaf interval).
    *   For each subsequent interval (`is_leaf == false`), the pass checks
        whether `selector` lies in `[lower, upper]` via
        `and(uge(selector, lower), ule(selector, upper))` and wraps the
        previously constructed select chain (`other`) in a 2-way `select`:
        `sel(in_bounds, cases=[other, if_in_range])`.

Example:
Consider a `select` operation where the selector `add.3` is a `bits[4]`
value proven by range analysis to lie in the single interval `[8, 11]`:

```
// Original IR snippet
fn func(x: bits[2]) -> bits[4] {
  zero_ext.1: bits[4] = zero_ext(x, new_bit_count=4)
  literal.2: bits[4] = literal(value=8)
  add.3: bits[4] = add(zero_ext.1, literal.2)
  // 16 cases (literal.4 through literal.19) for selector values 0..15:
  ret sel.20: bits[4] = sel(add.3, cases=[
    literal.4, literal.5, literal.6, literal.7, literal.8, literal.9,
    literal.10, literal.11, literal.12, literal.13, literal.14,
    literal.15, literal.16, literal.17, literal.18, literal.19
  ])
}
```

Because `add.3` only takes values in `[8, 11]`, `SparsifySelectPass` replaces
the 16-way `sel.20` with a 4-case `select` offset by the interval lower bound
(`8`):

```
// Optimized IR snippet
fn func(x: bits[2]) -> bits[4] {
  zero_ext.1: bits[4] = zero_ext(x, new_bit_count=4)
  literal.2: bits[4] = literal(value=8)
  add.3: bits[4] = add(zero_ext.1, literal.2)
  lower_bound: bits[4] = literal(value=8)
  offset: bits[4] = sub(add.3, lower_bound)
  zero: bits[4] = literal(value=0)
  ret sel.21: bits[4] = sel(offset,
      cases=[literal.12, literal.13, literal.14, literal.15],
      default=zero)
}
```

If the selector's `IntervalSet` contains multiple disjoint intervals, the
first (smallest) interval forms the leaf `select`, and each subsequent
interval wraps it in `sel(and(uge(selector, lower), ule(selector, upper)),
cases=[previous_chain, interval_select])`.


[Header](http://github.com/google/xls/tree/main/xls/passes/sparsify_select_pass.h)






## strength_red - Strength Reduction {#strength_red}


Replaces operations with equivalent cheaper operations. For example, an add
with no possible carries may be replaced with a bitwise OR.

!!! NOTE
    What follows was generated by the Gemini LLM. Not human verified.

The `StrengthReductionPass` is an optimization pass in XLS that improves
hardware efficiency by replacing computationally expensive operations with
equivalent, cheaper primitives. This reduces the area, critical-path delay,
and power consumption of the generated hardware by leveraging known constant
operands and bit-level value properties.

The pass traverses the IR in topological order and queries a
`UnionQueryEngine` combining `StatelessQueryEngine` and a context-cached
`PartialInfoQueryEngine` (wrapped in `CachedStateElementQueryEngine`) to
inspect known bits, leading/trailing zeros, and sign bits.

Key strength reductions performed by this pass include:

1.  **Replacement of Fully Known Nodes with Literals** (`NarrowingEnabled`):
    If the `QueryEngine` proves that a non-literal node with at least one
    user always evaluates to a constant value, it is replaced with a
    `literal` node.

2.  **Sinking Operations into `Select`s**:
    If a non-side-effecting, non-`invoke` operation has an operand that is a
    `sel` (`Select`) whose cases (and default, if present) are all known
    constants, the operation is sunk into the `sel` cases whenever:
    *   All other operands of the operation are also known constants, or
    *   The `sel` feeds the index, start offset, selector, or shift amount
        of an operation that simplifies when that operand is constant (1D
        `array_index`, `array_slice`, `bit_slice_update`,
        `dynamic_bit_slice`, `sel`, `priority_sel`, `shll`, `shra`, `shrl`),
    provided doing so does not widen the `sel` via a cheap widening op
    (`array`, `array_concat`, `concat`, `sign_ext`, `tuple`, `zero_ext`).

    ```
    // Original IR
    v1: bits[32] = sel(selector, cases=[const1, const2])
    v2: bits[32] = add(v1, const3)

    // Optimized IR
    v1_c1: bits[32] = add(const1, const3)
    v1_c2: bits[32] = add(const2, const3)
    v2: bits[32] = sel(selector, cases=[v1_c1, v1_c2])
    ```

3.  **Additions (`add`)**:
    *   **Addition with Zero**: `add(x, 0)` or `add(0, x)` is replaced with
        `x`.
    *   **Addition to Bitwise OR (No Carry)**: If at every bit position `i`,
        at least one operand is known to be `0`, no carry can be generated
        and `add(a, b)` is replaced with `or(a, b)`.
    *   **Adding a Value to Itself**: `add(a, a)` is replaced with
        `concat(bit_slice(a, start=0, width=W-1), 0:bits[1])`, which shifts
        left by 1 bit with zero logic delay.
    *   **Narrowing Low Known-Zero Bits** (`SplitsEnabled`): If either
        operand has `k > 0` known trailing zeros, only the upper `W - k` bits
        are added and concatenated with the lower `k` bits of the other
        operand.
    *   **Splitting Adders at Non-Propagating Carries** (`SplitsEnabled`):
        If both operands are known to be `0` at bit `i` (`i < W - 1`), a
        carry cannot propagate past bit `i`. The adder is split at bit
        `i + 1` into smaller independent adders whose results are
        concatenated.

4.  **Subtractions (`sub`)**:
    *   **Subtraction of Zero**: `sub(x, 0)` is replaced with `x`.
    *   **Subtracting from All-Ones**: `sub(all_ones, x)` is replaced with
        `not(x)`.
    *   **Narrowing Low Known Bits** (`SplitsEnabled`): If the LHS has `k`
        known trailing ones (more than the RHS's known trailing zeros), only
        the upper `W - k` bits are subtracted and concatenated with
        `not(bit_slice(rhs, start=0, width=k))`. Otherwise, if the RHS has
        `k > 0` known trailing zeros, only the upper `W - k` bits are
        subtracted and concatenated with `bit_slice(lhs, start=0, width=k)`.
    *   **Splitting Subtractors at Non-Propagating Borrows**
        (`SplitsEnabled`): If at bit `i` (`i < W - 1`) the LHS bit is known
        `1` and the RHS bit is known `0`, a borrow cannot propagate past bit
        `i`, so the subtractor is split at bit `i + 1` into smaller
        independent subtractors concatenated together.

5.  **Bitwise AND with a Contiguous Mask (`and`)** (`NarrowingEnabled`):
    A binary `and(x, mask)` where `mask` is known to have a single contiguous
    run of set bits (e.g., `0b001110`) is replaced with
    `concat(0, bit_slice(x, start=trailing_zeros, width=selected_bits), 0)`.

6.  **Single-Bit `Select` Expansion and Sign-Extension Detection**:
    *   **Exploding 1-Bit Muxes** (`SplitsEnabled`): A 1-bit `sel` with a
        1-bit selector `s` where at least one branch is a literal or equals
        `s` is expanded into `or(and(s, on_true), and(not(s), on_false))`.
    *   **`Select` to `SignExt`**: A `sel` with a 1-bit selector that chooses
        between all-zeros and all-ones is replaced with `sign_ext(s)` (or
        `sign_ext(not(s))` if inverted).

7.  **`SignExt` to `ZeroExt`**:
    If the MSB of the operand of `sign_ext(x)` is known to be `0`, the
    operation is replaced with `zero_ext(x)`.

8.  **`Gate` Simplification**:
    *   If `condition` is known `1`, `gate(cond, data)` is replaced with
        `data`.
    *   If `condition` is known `0` or `data` is known all-zeros, the `gate`
        is replaced with a zero `literal`.

9.  **Single-Bit `Add` / `Ne` and Small Comparisons**:
    *   1-bit `add(x, y)` and `ne(x, y)` are replaced with `xor(x, y)`.
    *   When `NarrowingEnabled`, unsigned comparisons against a power-of-two
        constant (`uge(x, 2^k)` and `ult(x, 2^k)`) are strength-reduced to
        comparing the upper `W - k` bits (`bit_slice(x, start=k, width=W-k)`)
        against `0` using `ne` or `eq`.
    *   When `NarrowingEnabled`, a 2-bit equality check against zero
        (`eq(x, 0b00)`) is replaced with
        `not(or(bit_slice(x, 0, 1), bit_slice(x, 1, 1)))`.

10. **Expensive Arithmetic with a Single Unknown Bit** (`NarrowingEnabled`):
    For `smul`, `umul`, `sdiv`, `udiv`, `smod`, and `umod` where across both
    operands only a single bit is unknown (all other bits are known
    constants), the pass evaluates the operation for both possible values of
    that bit using `InterpretNode` and replaces the arithmetic op with a
    `sel` driven by an `eq` comparison of the operand containing the unknown
    bit against one of its two constant completions.


[Header](http://github.com/google/xls/tree/main/xls/passes/strength_reduction_pass.h)






## table_switch - Table switch conversion {#table_switch}


TableSwitchPass converts chains of Select/PrioritySelect nodes into
ArrayIndex ops. These chains have the form:
sel.(N)(eq.X, literal.A, literal.B)
sel.(N+1)(eq.Y, sel.(N), literal.C)
sel.(N+2)(eq.Z, sel.(N+1), literal.D)
And so on. In these chains, eq.X, eq.Y, and eq.Z must all be `eq` or `ne`
comparisons of the same value against constant keys.

Current limitations:
 - Chains must contain at least 3 links.
 - Keys must fit in `uint64_t`, and matched values (plus the final
   fall-through value if the index space is not fully covered) must be
   literals.
 - Matched keys must cover either the entire index space or more than half
   of `[0, min(2^width, max_key + 2))`.
 - `Select` ops must be binary, and `PrioritySelect` selectors must be 1-bit
   or a `Concat` of 1-bit selectors.

!!! NOTE
    What follows was generated by the Gemini LLM. Not human verified.

The `TableSwitchPass` is an optimization pass in XLS that transforms cascaded
chains of `sel` and `priority_sel` nodes into direct `array_index` table
lookups on an array literal. Replacing a chain of conditional branches
comparing a common index against constant keys with a single constant-array
lookup simplifies control logic and improves hardware area and delay.

**How it Works**:

1.  **Chain Matching (`MatchLinks`)**:
    *   The pass traverses nodes in reverse topological order (`Use`-before-
        `Def`, via `context.ReverseTopoSort(f)`) and records interior links
        in a `transformed` set so it matches outermost lookup-chain roots
        first and skips interior links already folded into an outer table. It
        uses a `StatelessQueryEngine` to resolve constant `uint64_t` keys.
    *   Each link in the chain is either:
        *   A binary `sel` or 1-bit `priority_sel` whose selector compares a
            common `index` node against a constant `uint64_t` `key` using
            `eq` or `ne`, selecting a `literal` value on match and forwarding
            to the `next` node on mismatch, or
        *   A multi-case `priority_sel` whose selector is a `concat` of 1-bit
            `eq`/`ne` comparisons against the same `index` node (with `ne`
            only permitted on the final case), which contributes multiple
            consecutive links to the chain. If only a suffix of a
            `priority_sel`'s cases starts the chain (at `first_case > 0`),
            the prefix cases are preserved in a truncated `priority_sel`
            whose default value becomes the new `array_index`.
    *   Chains with 2 or fewer links (`links.size() <= 2`) are skipped as too
        short to benefit from table conversion.

2.  **Table Construction (`LinksToTable`)**:
    *   The pass walks the chain from outermost to innermost link, recording
        the first `Literal` value associated with each `uint64_t` key (later
        duplicate keys in the chain are unreachable and ignored).
    *   **Full Index Space Coverage**: If the index width is `< 63` bits and
        the matched keys cover all `2^width` possible index values, the final
        fall-through (`else`) value is dead and need not be a literal; the
        pass emits an array literal of size `2^width`.
    *   **Partial / Sparse Coverage with Saturation**: Otherwise, the final
        fall-through node must be a `Literal` (`else_value`). Leveraging XLS
        `array_index` out-of-bounds saturation semantics (where any index
        `>= size - 1` clamps to the last element), the pass bounds the table
        size to `min(2^width, max_key + 2)`. If more than half of the entries
        in `[0, table_size)` are explicitly matched (`map.size() * 2 >
        table_size`), any missing indices (gaps) and the saturating final
        slot are filled with `else_value`.

3.  **Replacement**:
    The pass creates a `literal` array containing the table entries and
    replaces the root of the chain with `array_index(array_literal,
    indices=[index])`.

**Example**:

```
// Original IR
fn main(index: bits[32]) -> bits[32] {
  literal.0: bits[32] = literal(value=0)
  literal.1: bits[32] = literal(value=1)
  literal.2: bits[32] = literal(value=2)
  literal.10: bits[32] = literal(value=10)
  literal.20: bits[32] = literal(value=20)
  literal.30: bits[32] = literal(value=30)
  literal.99: bits[32] = literal(value=99)
  eq.4: bits[1] = eq(index, literal.0)
  eq.5: bits[1] = eq(index, literal.1)
  eq.6: bits[1] = eq(index, literal.2)
  sel.7: bits[32] = sel(eq.4, cases=[literal.99, literal.10])
  sel.8: bits[32] = sel(eq.5, cases=[sel.7, literal.20])
  ret sel.9: bits[32] = sel(eq.6, cases=[sel.8, literal.30])
}

// Optimized IR (after dead code elimination)
fn main(index: bits[32]) -> bits[32] {
  array_literal: bits[32][4] = literal(value=[10, 20, 30, 99])
  ret array_index.10: bits[32] = array_index(array_literal, indices=[index])
}
```


[Header](http://github.com/google/xls/tree/main/xls/passes/table_switch_pass.h)






## token_dependency - Convert data dependencies between effectful operations into token dependencies {#token_dependency}


Pass which turns data dependencies between certain effectful operations into
token dependencies. In particular, transitive data dependencies between
receives and other effectful ops are turned into token dependencies whenever
no such token dependency already exists.

!!! NOTE
    What follows was generated by the Gemini LLM. Not human verified.

The `TokenDependencyPass` ensures that ordering constraints implied by data
dependencies between `receive` operations and downstream side-effecting
token-consuming operations (such as `send`, `receive`, or `assert`) are
explicitly captured in the token dependency graph.

For example, if a `send` operation consumes a value derived from a `receive`
operation's payload, but subsequent algebraic optimizations prove that the
expression is independent of the received value (e.g., multiplied by zero or
masked off), later passes could eliminate the data dependency. Without an
explicit token path from the `receive` to the `send`, the scheduler could
reorder the two I/O operations and violate program semantics.

**How it Works**:

1.  **Token Provenance & Transitive Closure**: The pass runs
    `TokenProvenanceAnalysis` on the `FunctionBase` to build the direct token
    dependency graph over side-effecting operations and `after_all` nodes,
    and computes its `TransitiveClosure`.
2.  **Data Dependency Search**: For each `receive` operation `a`, the pass
    performs a depth-first search over the data dependency graph to find all
    downstream side-effecting token operations `b` that are not already
    reachable from `a` in the token transitive closure.
3.  **Transitive Pruning**: If operation `c` is token-dependent on operation
    `b`, and both `b` and `c` are data-dependent on `receive` `a`, the pass
    prunes `a` from `c`'s required set (`minimal_io_to_data_supplying_io`),
    since adding a token edge from `a` to `b` transitively orders `a` before
    `c`.
4.  **Token Rewiring**: For each remaining pair `(io, supplying_receive)`,
    the pass extracts the token output of `supplying_receive` via
    `tuple_index(supplying_receive, index=0)` and combines it with `io`'s
    existing token operand using a new `after_all` node.

**Example**:

```
// Original IR
chan test_channel(
  bits[32], id=0, kind=streaming, ops=send_receive,
  flow_control=ready_valid)

top proc main(__state: (), init={()}) {
  __token: token = literal(value=token, id=1000)
  receive.1: (token, bits[32]) = receive(__token, channel=test_channel)
  tuple_index.2: token = tuple_index(receive.1, index=0)
  tuple_index.3: bits[32] = tuple_index(receive.1, index=1)
  send.4: token = send(__token, tuple_index.3, channel=test_channel)
  after_all.5: token = after_all(send.4, tuple_index.2)
  tuple.6: () = tuple()
  next (tuple.6)
}

// Optimized IR
top proc main(__state: (), init={()}) {
  __token: token = literal(value=token, id=1000)
  receive.1: (token, bits[32]) = receive(__token, channel=test_channel)
  tuple_index.2: token = tuple_index(receive.1, index=0)
  tuple_index.3: bits[32] = tuple_index(receive.1, index=1)
  tuple_index.7: token = tuple_index(receive.1, index=0)
  after_all.8: token = after_all(tuple_index.7, __token)
  send.4: token = send(after_all.8, tuple_index.3, channel=test_channel)
  after_all.5: token = after_all(send.4, tuple_index.2)
  tuple.6: () = tuple()
  next (tuple.6)
}
```


[Header](http://github.com/google/xls/tree/main/xls/passes/token_dependency_pass.h)






## token_simp - Simplify token networks {#token_simp}


Pass that simplifies token networks. For example, if an AfterAll node has
operands where one operand is an ancestor of another in the token graph, then
the ancestor can be omitted. Similarly, duplicate operands can be removed and
AfterAlls with one operand can be replaced with their operand.

!!! NOTE
    What follows was generated by the Gemini LLM. Not human verified.

The `TokenSimplificationPass` simplifies the token dependency network within
a function or proc. Token networks enforce ordering constraints between
side-effecting operations (such as `send`, `receive`, and `assert`). By
removing redundant token edges and canonicalizing `min_delay` annotations,
this pass reduces control complexity and simplifies downstream scheduling.

If any node in the `FunctionBase` has a type containing more than one token
(e.g., a tuple containing multiple tokens), the pass conservatively bails out
without modifying the IR.

Otherwise, the pass executes a sequence of subpasses on `after_all` and
`min_delay` operations:

1.  **Simplifying `min_delay` Operations**:
    *   **Trivial `min_delay`**: A `min_delay(tok, delay=0)` is replaced with
        `tok`. Similarly, `min_delay(after_all(), delay=X)` on an empty
        `after_all()` is replaced with `after_all()`.

        ```
        // Original IR
        min_delay.1: token = min_delay(tok, delay=0)

        // Optimized IR
        // Uses of min_delay.1 are replaced directly with tok.
        ```

    *   **Collapsing Nested `min_delay`s**: Consecutive `min_delay`
        operations are merged by summing their delays:
        `min_delay(min_delay(tok, delay=1), delay=2)` becomes
        `min_delay(tok, delay=3)`.

        ```
        // Original IR
        min_delay.1: token = min_delay(tok, delay=1)
        min_delay.2: token = min_delay(min_delay.1, delay=2)

        // Optimized IR
        min_delay.3: token = min_delay(tok, delay=3)
        ```

    *   **Pushing `min_delay` Down Through `after_all`**: If all operands of
        a non-empty `after_all` are `min_delay` nodes with positive delays,
        the minimum common delay `d_min` is factored out after the
        `after_all`, leaving residual `min_delay(..., delay=d - d_min)` nodes
        only for operands with `d > d_min`.

        ```
        // Original IR
        min_delay.1: token = min_delay(tok_a, delay=1)
        min_delay.2: token = min_delay(tok_b, delay=3)
        after_all.3: token = after_all(min_delay.1, min_delay.2)

        // Optimized IR
        min_delay.4: token = min_delay(tok_b, delay=2)
        after_all.5: token = after_all(tok_a, min_delay.4)
        min_delay.6: token = min_delay(after_all.5, delay=1)
        ```

2.  **Simplifying `after_all` Operations**:
    *   **Collapsing Nested `after_all`s**: In reverse topological order, if
        an `after_all` node has no implicit uses and all of its users are
        also `after_all` nodes, its operands are flattened directly into each
        user `after_all`.

        ```
        // Original IR
        after_all.1: token = after_all(tok_a, tok_b)
        after_all.2: token = after_all(after_all.1, tok_c)

        // Optimized IR
        after_all.3: token = after_all(tok_c, tok_a, tok_b)
        ```

    *   **Pruning Overlapping (Ancestor) `after_all` Operands**: If an
        `after_all` has operands `x` and `y` where `x` transitively depends
        on `y` through token-carrying nodes (conservatively stopping at
        `invoke` nodes so the pass is safe before function inlining, and
        bounding traversal by topological index), `y` is redundant and
        replaced by another operand of the `after_all`.
    *   **Deduplicating Operands**: Duplicate operands in an `after_all` are
        removed (with remaining unique operands sorted by node ID).
    *   **Single-Operand `after_all`**: An `after_all(tok)` with a single
        operand is replaced directly with `tok`.

        ```
        // Original IR
        send.2: token = send(tok, data, channel=ch)
        send.3: token = send(send.2, data, channel=ch)
        after_all.4: token = after_all(tok, send.2, send.3)

        // Optimized IR
        // tok and send.2 are ancestors of send.3; after pruning,
        // deduplication, and single-operand removal, after_all.4 is
        // replaced directly with send.3.
        ```

If any simplification modifies the IR, `CollapseMinDelay` is run one final
time to merge any `min_delay` operations that became adjacent after
`after_all` removal.

## useless_assert_remove - Remove useless (always true) asserts {#useless_assert_remove}


Pass which removes asserts that have a literal 1 as the condition, meaning
they are never triggered. Rewires tokens to ensure nothing breaks.

!!! NOTE
    What follows was generated by the Gemini LLM. Not human verified.

The `UselessAssertRemovalPass` eliminates `assert` operations whose condition
is statically known to be true (`1`), since such assertions can never fail
at runtime or in simulation.

**How it Works**:

1.  **Condition Analysis**: The pass traverses the IR in topological order
    and queries a `StatelessQueryEngine` (`KnownValueAsBits`) on each
    `assert` node's `condition` operand.
2.  **Token Rewiring and Removal**: If the `condition` is known to be `1`
    (`IsOne()`), all uses of the `assert` node's output token are replaced
    directly with the `assert`'s input `token` operand, and the `assert`
    node is removed from the `FunctionBase`.

**Example**:

```
// Original IR
fn f(tkn: token) -> token {
  literal.1: bits[1] = literal(value=1)
  ret assert.2: token = assert(tkn, literal.1, message="always passes")
}

// Optimized IR
fn f(tkn: token) -> token {
  ret tkn
}
```


[Header](http://github.com/google/xls/tree/main/xls/passes/useless_assert_removal_pass.h)






## useless_io_remove - Remove useless send/receive {#useless_io_remove}


Pass which removes sends/receives that have literal false as their condition.
Also removes the condition from sends/receives that have literal true as
their condition.

!!! NOTE
    What follows was generated by the Gemini LLM. Not human verified.

The `UselessIORemovalPass` simplifies predicated `send` and `receive`
operations across all procs in a `Package` when their `predicate` operand is
statically known to be `0` (false) or `1` (true) according to a
`StatelessQueryEngine`.

First, the pass builds a package-wide map (`ComputeChannelMaps`) tracking
all `send` and `receive` operations associated with each `ChannelRef`. It
then traverses each proc in topological order and applies the following
transformations to predicated I/O nodes:

1.  **Removal or Simplification of False-Predicated I/O (`predicate == 0`)**:
    *   **`send` with `predicate == 0`**:
        *   If there is at least one other `send` remaining on the same
            channel, the disabled `send` is removed and its uses are replaced
            with its input `token` operand.
        *   If it is the **last** `send` on that channel, removing it would
            leave the channel without a sender. Instead, the `send` is kept
            and its `data` operand is replaced with a zero literal
            (`ZeroOfType`) so dead upstream data computation can be removed.
    *   **`receive` with `predicate == 0`**:
        *   If there is at least one other `receive` remaining on the same
            channel, the disabled `receive` is removed and replaced with a
            `tuple` containing `(token, zero_data)` for blocking receives, or
            `(token, zero_data, 0)` (with a `0` valid bit) for non-blocking
            receives.

    ```
    // Original IR (assuming another send exists on my_chan)
    literal.1: bits[1] = literal(value=0)
    send.2: token = send(tkn, data, predicate=literal.1, channel=my_chan)

    // Optimized IR
    // Uses of send.2 are replaced directly with tkn.
    ```

2.  **Simplification of True-Predicated I/O (`predicate == 1`)**:
    If a `send` or `receive` has a predicate known to be `1`, the redundant
    `predicate` operand is stripped, converting the operation into an
    unpredicated `send` or `receive` on the same channel.

    ```
    // Original IR
    literal.1: bits[1] = literal(value=1)
    receive.2: (token, bits[32]) = receive(tkn, predicate=literal.1,
        channel=my_chan)

    // Optimized IR
    receive.3: (token, bits[32]) = receive(tkn, channel=my_chan)
    ```
